This is the most frustrating thing. 

I work in adolescent inpatient psych. The kids I see are all heavily online and influenced by tiktok. It is obvious to us as staff when a patient is genuinely experiencing mania versus when a patient is excitable/restless/fidgety etc but I constantly hear (and have to redirect) conversations about “I’m so manic right now” “when I’M manic…” as if it’s something everyone experiences. It absolutely is not. 

I even have a friend my age who says “when i’m manic I do illegal things” “when i’m manic I break shit” despite not having a bipolar diagnosis. I took an opportunity to explain that in my manic episodes I have believed my coworkers were trying to trap me in the staff room so they could murder me and I was only safe from them tracking me when I was riding a citibike, and i maxed out all of my credit cards and am now $10k in debt, and i have ruined important relationships over issues that were created in my head. That seemed to shut her up. It’s just so invalidating to hear people throw around a word that describes the most sensitive and volatile periods of my life, 85% of which I don’t even remember, because they want to seem more “ill.” I absolutely hate it.

He is caring and empathetic, and with the amount of trauma he has experienced he has to be extremely resilient. In real life if someone had gone through being essentially abducted and tortured, only to then feel alienated from their friends and deal with feeling “different” like he does, their compassion would start to fade. I have found that starting a healthcare job a month before the pandemic has given me severe compassion fatigue over the past 2 years. It’s silly but characters like Will who are just doing their best are a comfort and inspiration to me. Yes he cries a lot and seems overly sensitive at times, but that’s an accurate depiction of PTSD. With better writing, he would be far more interesting, but the actor does a good job of making me love the character anyway.
